I know the basics of SQL, data manipulation, selection, user management and so on. I know the basics of database design too (i.e. the normal forms).

What I'm less confident with is how to get my programs to interact with the database in an efficient way. I can get a query run via a cursor in a language of my choice passing in a direct SQL statement. How would I try to generate a weekly report given a query I've designed? Would stored procedures be the right way to go? What are the alternatives?
Can someone point me to a resource for learning how to properly interact with a SQL database?

I guess I could add on to why I've found this as a need and what resources I've looked at so far.

I've gone through the various codecademy pages and found them extremely bare bones, you can get through these in a week and they don't really prepare you for anything aside from running your first database and querying directly. I've gone through hours of Microsoft's SQL tutorials on their website but to continue doing so would likely take a full year given how much is on there and any direction is appreciated. The pacing could use some work.

I've looked through edx and coursera offerings. However, any time SQL is mentioned we always stop short of learning the syntax of a query, maybe a few sentences on design and ultimately quit before doing anything substantial. I don't think I'd even heard stored procedures said before. You might get a few mentions of transactions if you are lucky.

In general: learning resources I've looked at seem to look at SQL (and it's variants) as a standalone tool when really a database is useless without other languages to power it or manipulate it's data. This part I'm struggling with designing and implementing.

I think at this point you're more out of the prescriptive part of learning SQL. It's a tool that can be applied to almost every problem (most things need to persist data at some point), and each application of it is going to run into its own weird, specific issues. There isn't going to be a silver bullet guide that covers every possible use case I don't think.

You mention too that it's a bit useless without another language to interact with it- this is true to an extent, but sort of overlooks what databases servers are and do. The server is where your data is actually being stored, and you then send that server queries from your actual application, written in a language that has a driver that can talk to your DB. These queries can do everything from save new data down, update existing data, pull down saved data, etc. The DB itself just defines ways to store tabular data, update that data, retrieve that data, and relates tables to one another. There are a couple other fancy things (stored procs, functions, views, indexes) that can help you pull your data in. But, the DB doesn't really "do" anything but store and relate your stuff together.

With all that being said, if you're interested in actually learning up on that weirder, more specific stuff, I'd just roll a simple DB server and start rigging up a basic application. You mentioned generating a weekly report based on a stored proc- I think this is a fantastic idea, it gets a bit into the weeds without sounding terribly complicated.

First step would be to start storing info related to whatever you want to report on. From here, it might be interesting to try to start writing a raw query that selects according to a date range (a couple of WHERE clauses should do the trick). Once you get that rigged up, try wrapping it into a stored proc that takes a startDate/endDate parameter. Could be worth now trying to compare the two solutions- see which (if either) is more efficient from a run-time standpoint, determine which is easier for you as a developer to actually work with in your code base, etc.

Again, it's hard to provide specific suggestions because those things are so terribly, terribly application specific. Most applications need a way to store and retrieve data somehow, but how that application actually handles the storage/retrieval is a lot tougher to just generalize.

Honestly I think that's a pretty common problem. I could probably sit down some Saturday, start going through some tutorials for some lang I've never used, and be able to make a syntactically correct thing that does nothing by the end of Sunday. That doesn't mean that I "know" that language at all, though. They all have weird quirks and specialties and ways of doing things, but they're all really just tools for solving other problems.

I try to get around that by trying to come up with some actual problem to solve first- then I go find what looks like a good (or at least remotely appropriate) tool for it and just suffer through till it starts to click. I find I actually start learning those quirks and specialties better instead of just sticking to the "this is how you add numbers" type of stuff.

And as for your project- I know that Python, C and PHP can all talk to MySQL. You mentioned not knowing when to use stored procs specifically- this is a perfect usecase for it. If you have some feature that you want to hit from every environment (say, loading up some news article with some JOIN'ed in other tables- something more complex than just a basic SELECT query), you could create a stored procedure that takes in a param or two and does all the heavy lifting. Now, instead of having some big, ugly SQL query copy/pasted across 3 codebases, you have 3 calls into your one stored proc. If you need to update what that query returns, you can do it in one place instead of multiple.
